title: Better your own dharma
hookLine: better your own work done imperfectly than someone else's done well
carry: better your own dharma, done imperfectly

cards: Somebody online is rebuilding houses after a flood. Somebody else runs a soup kitchen, fosters dogs, teaches kids to read.
It's inspiring, and it can also leave a person frozen, scrolling through other people's good work and wondering whether their own is too small to count. The Gita has a verse for that exact paralysis.
Krishna says it in chapter three, and nearly again near the end of the book. Today: which service is actually yours.

teach.b: In paraphrase: better your own dharma, even done imperfectly, than the dharma of another done well. The word is svadharma. Sva means one's own.

teach.h: SVADHARMA: THE DUTY THAT IS YOURS.
teach.b: Dharma is a big word, duty, right order, the way a thing is meant to work; here it's the duty that belongs to your actual place in life.

In the Gita's story, Arjuna is a warrior who has just said he'd rather live as a beggar than fight, and Krishna is telling him not to trade his own hard task for someone else's that looks easier or holier.
In chapter eighteen the line comes back: by doing the work that belongs to your own nature, you don't incur fault.
There it comes right after verses on the duties of the four varnas, the classes of the old social order, each said to arise from its own nature.

teach.h: READERS HAVE ARGUED OVER HOW TO APPLY IT.
teach.b: Hindu readers have argued about how to apply that. Older readings tie svadharma to varna, caste, and stage of life.
Some modern Hindu teachers read it more as the duty that fits your nature, your gifts, your situation, and that reading has its critics too. And notice the word imperfectly.
Krishna isn't promising your service will be impressive. He's saying it will be yours.
So the first question changes: not what's the most admirable work out there, but what's mine to do.
The parent of a small child may have a year of service that looks like patience at bedtime and one shift a month somewhere else.
A nurse might serve by not cutting corners on a tired night. Someone with a car might be the one who drives. The flood houses are real and good.
They just might belong to someone else.

how: Hindu teachers read the Gita's svadharma verses in more than one way, some tying them to caste and stage of life and others to a person's nature and situation; some people turn to the verse when weighing what kind of work or service is theirs.

o: a duty you swap for one that looks holier
the most admirable work that anyone could choose
the duty that's truly yours, even done imperfectly

games.q: your own dharma — tap the pairs.
p: the duty that belongs to you

s: the Gita says another person's dharma, done well, is better than your own done badly
it says the opposite: better your own, even done imperfectly.
the svadharma line appears in chapter three and again in chapter eighteen
Krishna says nearly the same thing twice.
Hindu readers all apply svadharma the same way
older readings tie it to caste and stage of life; other readers emphasize nature and situation.

games.q: you're Arjuna. another kind of life looks easier, maybe even holier, than the hard task that's yours. what does Krishna advise?
o: take the other path; it's done better there.
stay with your own dharma, even done imperfectly.
wait until you can do both perfectly.
games.why: Krishna says your own dharma, even imperfect, is better than another's done well, and repeats it in chapter eighteen.

practice: Let three things come up without judging them: something you're simply good at; a place you're already in, a group, a route you drive; and a person who already relies on you.

Breathe with each and see where the three overlap, since that overlap may be the start of your own dharma of service, imperfect and yours. If you pray, you can ask the one you pray to for clarity about it.

wordCard.voice: Svadharma. One's own dharma, the service that belongs to your own life, better done imperfectly than another's done well.

orig.note: Sanskrit, in Devanagari: svadharma, one's own dharma, from Gita 3.35 and 18.47.

carryVoice: Your line: better your own dharma, done imperfectly. Tomorrow, three ways to give the same gift. Day nine hundred seventy, done.

sources.ref: Bhagavad Gita 3.35 (better one's own dharma, though imperfect, than another's well performed)
Bhagavad Gita 18.47 (the line repeated; doing the work of one's own nature incurs no fault)
Bhagavad Gita 2.5 (Arjuna: better to live on alms than to kill his elders)
